newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Gasoline stock fall seen tempered in APIs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Gasoline stock fall seen tempered in APIs.

text.p: REUTER SURVEY ESTIMATES* ACTUAL STOCKS FOR
UTILIZATION..... DN 0.50 PCT PT 96.7 DN 0.1 PCT PT
*NB - The survey estimate is derived by omitting the high and low forecast and averaging the rest, with a sample of at least six.

Tuesday evening's oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) is expected, once again, to show feverish gasoline demand, but the data may end up showing a comparatively tepid one to two million barrel fall in gasoline stocks, dealers said.

"There should be a seasonal decline in gasoline stocks, but refinery runs will be high enough and imports should be strong enough to temper the draw down," said Jim Ritterbusch, trader with Sweeney Oil in Illinois.
Refinery utilization rates are seen easing only about a half percentage point from its torrid 96.7 percent level seen for the week ended July 18. Tuesday's data reflects the week ended July 25.
Crude stocks are expected to decline one to three million barrels while distillate stocks are seen rising one to two million barrels.
Some dealers refuse to rule out a bullish surprise in gasoline stocks.
"There are estimates out there that peg the gasoline draw near five million barrels," said one New York gasoline dealer on the NYMEX floor.
Indeed, gasoline demand has averaged a lofty 8.7 million barrels a day (bpd) over the past month as the solid U.S. economy has encouraged more holiday driving during the summer, dealers said.
The strong implied demand figure has in fact reflected inventory shifts to gasoline stations in anticipation of demand rather than demand itself, some dealers argue.

"Demand has been overstated," said Sweeney Oil's Ritterbusch. Gasoline imports could also stay near the 458,000 bpd seen in last week's figures due to a more attractive arbitrage recently from Europe.
Imports of crude, meanwhile, are expected to ease from a high 8.1 million bpd when refineries are demanding more crude, decreasing supply.

Distillate stocks, comprised of heating oil and diesel, should see a correction in diesel demand. Diesel demand jumped the week ended July 18, sending distillate stocks down 1.2 million barrels at a time when those stocks usually build.
